_comment: Reviewed suppressions for tools/supply-chain/scan-dependencies.sh, which scans the
dependency trees this application actually ships: pom.xml (Maven) and
ui/package-lock.json (npm). See ADR-050.
SCOPE. This file governs HIGH and CRITICAL findings only, because those are the only
severities the scan gates on. A MEDIUM or LOW must never be listed: the scan does not
fail on one, so an entry for one would be unfireable, and an unfireable entry rots into
a claim nobody checks. If a MEDIUM matters enough to write prose about, fix it instead.
This file is deliberately SEPARATE from accepted-advisories.json, which is the allowlist
for audit-plugins.sh. Different scanner, different identifier space, and above all a
different subject: this file is about code that reaches production, that one is about
the OpenCode plugins on a developer's machine. Do not merge them, and do not copy an
entry from one to the other -- a reachability trace written about a developer tool is
not a trace through the deployed application.
KEY FORMAT is 'ID@module', for example 'CVE-2026-59889@tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind'.
The module is part of the key rather than only a field, because one advisory genuinely can
hit two packages at once: on 2026-08-22 CVE-2026-59889 was reported against BOTH
com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind 2.21.4 and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind
3.1.4 in the same scan. Keyed by bare ID, suppressing one would have silently suppressed
the other. This is a deliberate divergence from accepted-advisories.json, which keys by
bare GHSA.
WHAT AN ENTRY MEANS. Not 'we know about this'. It means a human read the advisory, traced
the vulnerable code path through this repository's actual runtime, and established that it
is not reached -- or that it is reached but no fixed version exists in any range we can
adopt. Name the file, the symbol and the guard in 'reachability'. 'Not exploitable in our
use case' with no trace is not a reachability argument and must be rejected in review.
PREFER THE UPGRADE. Every finding closed under EOP-89 was closed by a patch-level version
override in pom.xml, not by an entry here, and that is the expected outcome. An entry is
the exception, and a permanent one is a bug: 'no_fix_available' must say why no in-range
upgrade exists, and if one appears later the entry must go.
AN ENTRY IS A LIABILITY, NOT A DISMISSAL. The scan fails in both directions. An unlisted
HIGH or CRITICAL fails. A listed entry whose module or severity no longer matches what the
scanner reports fails. A listed entry that is NO LONGER REPORTED AT ALL fails, and the fix
is to DELETE it -- never to widen it. And a listed entry whose 'expires' date has passed
fails even though everything else still matches, which is the point of the date: it forces
the trace to be re-argued rather than inherited. Deleting a stale entry is routine; adding
one is not.
EXPIRY. 'expires' is a YYYY-MM-DD date and is mandatory. On and after that date the entry
stops suppressing and the build goes red. Six months is the default horizon; choose less if
the reachability argument depends on something likely to move sooner. Do not extend a date
without re-tracing -- editing the number is a five-second change that silently converts a
reviewed judgement into an unreviewed one.
WHAT THIS CANNOT DO. Unreachable today is not unreachable tomorrow. Nothing here notices a
dependency bump that starts calling the vulnerable API: the scanner still reports the same
advisory against the same module at the same severity, the entry still matches, and the
suppression holds while the premise underneath it has quietly failed. Only the expiry date
bounds that, and it bounds it loosely. Re-verify the trace whenever a version in the chain
moves, and prefer moving off the dependency to carrying an entry indefinitely.
The 'advisories' object is empty, and that is the correct steady state.
